title: The Chumscrubber
full_review:
There's just enough reality in "The Chumscrubber" (Newmarket), the mordantly funny but also deeply disturbing satire about troubled high school students, to make you seriously worry about the state of contemporary suburbia.

Jamie Bell, star of the English charmer "Billy Elliott," gets better in every film, and here he plays Dean, the son of motivational author Dr. Bill Stiffle (William Fichtner) and a vitamin promoter (Allison Janney), who discovers his best friend Troy -- the supplier of "feel-good" pills at school -- dead and hanging by a noose in the house, while Troy's distracted mother, Mrs. Johnson (Glenn Close), blithely entertains her guests at a party outside.

Dean leaves without revealing what he's seen. He believes no one will care, a presumption not far from the truth. This apparent detachment prompts his father, clueless about dealing with his son, to prescribe, ironically, pills for the boy, which the inwardly traumatized Dean is only too glad to pop.

The troublemaking kids at Dean's school, led by the sadistic Billy (Justin Chatwin), Lee (Lou Taylor Pucci) and Crystal (Camilla Belle), pressure Dean to find Troy's stash of drugs. When Dean refuses, the gang decides to kidnap Dean's younger brother, Charlie (Rory Culkin), to force Dean to acquiesce.

Instead, they kidnap the wrong Charlie (Thomas Curtis), the son of Terri (Rita Wilson), a self-absorbed (like every other adult in the film) designer, about to marry Michael (Ralph Fiennes), the town's ineffectual and emotionally damaged mayor. Charlie's birth father is local bumbling cop Lou (John Heard).

Though the kidnappers at first treat their hostage reasonably well, and the boy even seems to enjoy his adventure, danger lurks, as Billy is a vicious loose cannon. When Dean learns of the scheme, he reluctantly overcomes his natural apathy to try to effect Charlie's release.

Meanwhile, the shell-shocked Mrs. Johnson plans her son's memorial service on the same day as Terri and Michael's wedding.

All the teens are completely left to their own devices, with their preoccupied, materialistic, uncaring, permissive and downright inept parents at sea. The teens can gain entry into anyone's house merely by spouting the catchphrase, "It's for school." Though the drug use is appalling, the parents are just as bad, seeing pills, vitamins and self-help books as panaceas for everything.

Even when various parents learn that young Charlie is being held against his will, they fail to recognize that it's a real kidnapping, or to behave responsibly. At one point, Mrs. Stiffle suggests to Dean that they switch parent-child roles; indeed, the adults seem scarcely more mature than their offspring.

The adults don't even relate to each other. Michael is clearly going through a profound personal crisis, but Terri jabbers away, unaware of his inner turmoil. Mrs. Johnson's loss of Troy has her yearning for empathy which never comes. There's a brilliant scene when Mrs. Johnson tries to return a casserole dish to Mrs. Stiffle, though the dish was, in fact, clearly never loaned in the first place.

First-time director Arie Posin's searing indictment of aloof, disengaged parents and alienated youths is overly simplistic, but generates a downright creepy sense of menace. The script is by first-timer Zac Stanford.

Though the message and "moral" are good ones, the film feels somewhat lightweight, almost trite, in texture.

But there's no denying it's finely acted by Bell, Close, Fiennes, Janney and the rest of the cast which includes Jason Isaacs, Caroline Goodall and Carrie-Anne Moss, and ends on a satisfyingly redemptive note of considerable poignancy. Most of the characters are one-dimensional types, but that suits Posin's purpose.

The off-putting title refers to a headless character in a videogame, meant presumably to be emblematic of the superficial pop culture at large.

For all its glibness, "The Chumscrubber" can be viewed as a sort of "Rebel Without a Cause" for the new millennium, and makes its points well, if a bit obviously.

The film contains profanity and rough language, crude expressions, underage drug use and smoking, brief violence with blood, a sexual situation with brief partial nudity, and suicide. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
